output.brief:
The jump in chilled write-offs is mainly an internal problem, not a Haverlow problem. Since the night receiving team went from six to four people in week 31, night pallets have taken about 3h50 to reach the chambers, up from 44 minutes. Day-shift put-away is unchanged. Staging lanes are unrefrigerated and run 15–17°C overnight. Haverlow's trailer data shows loads arriving at 2.4–3.5°C with no alarms. The doors were emptied within about 40 minutes of opening, well before receipt was confirmed at 02:30–03:20. So the 6.5–8°C probe readings were taken after the product had warmed on the dock, and they don't show supplier abuse. The chambers held temperature. Night write-off rates rose to about 3% for every supplier, while day rates stayed at about 0.6%.

Next step: restore the night team to six and cap dock-to-chamber time, tracked weekly from scan data. Drop the chargeback and the volume shift, and keep the probe. Also sample Corriebank's claims against delivery lots and receiving shift. Some of the rise in credits may come from warm product and some from easier claiming, and we can't yet say how much of each. I'm fairly confident in the main finding.
output.methodChoice: Collected X3 (shift-level dock-to-chamber times) and X4 (independent trailer telematics) to discriminate the warming-in-DC explanation from the supplier-abuse explanation.
